title: Authentication: Sessions, JWT & OAuth
summary: How users prove who they are: **session cookies** vs **JWTs**, where to store tokens (httpOnly cookies vs localStorage), and **OAuth/OIDC** for third-party login. Auth bugs are security bugs.

subtopics.title: Session cookies
subtopics.explanation: The server stores session state and hands the browser an opaque session id in an httpOnly cookie; simple and easy to revoke.

subtopics.title: JWT
subtopics.explanation: A signed token carrying claims that the server can verify without a lookup (stateless). Powerful but harder to revoke and risky if stored where JS can read it.

subtopics.title: Where to store tokens
subtopics.explanation: Prefer httpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies so script can't read the token (mitigates XSS token theft); avoid localStorage for sensitive tokens.

subtopics.title: OAuth / OIDC
subtopics.explanation: Delegated auth: 'log in with Google' — the provider authenticates the user and returns tokens/identity to your app without you handling passwords.

foundations.overview: Authentication is how a user proves identity and stays logged in. The two common models are server sessions (the server keeps state, the browser holds an opaque session id in a cookie) and JWTs (a signed, stateless token the server verifies). A central frontend decision is where to keep the credential: httpOnly cookies keep it out of JavaScript's reach (safer against XSS), while localStorage is convenient but exposed. OAuth/OIDC delegates login to a provider so you never handle passwords.
foundations.formalDefinition: Mechanisms for establishing and maintaining identity: session cookies, JWTs, cookie/storage strategy, token refresh, and delegated auth via OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect.
foundations.whyItMatters: Auth mistakes are security incidents — stolen tokens, session fixation, or leaking credentials. It's also a top senior interview area (and the natural companion to security).
foundations.mentalModel: A wristband at an event: a session cookie is a numbered band the door staff look up; a JWT is a tamper-proof band with your details printed and signed on it.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser attaches cookies automatically (subject to SameSite) and cannot read httpOnly cookies from script — the basis of safe token storage.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Login flows, protecting authed routes, refreshing tokens, and 'log in with Google/GitHub' via OAuth.
foundations.businessImpact: Account takeover is among the most damaging incidents; robust auth protects users and the business.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Choosing sessions vs JWT and correct cookie flags prevents whole classes of vulnerabilities and simplifies logout/revocation.
foundations.performanceImpact: Stateless JWTs avoid a session lookup per request but shift cost to token size and refresh handling.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Store the JWT in localStorage for convenience.
commonMisconceptions.reality: localStorage is readable by any script, so an XSS bug leaks the token; prefer httpOnly cookies for sensitive tokens.

commonMisconceptions.myth: JWTs are more secure than sessions.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They're stateless, not inherently more secure — they're harder to revoke and dangerous if stored insecurely. Choose per needs.

theory.question: Where should you store an auth token in the browser, and why?
theory.directAnswer: For sensitive tokens, prefer an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. httpOnly means JavaScript can't read it, so an XSS bug can't steal it; Secure keeps it to HTTPS; SameSite mitigates CSRF. localStorage is convenient and works for bearer-token APIs, but it's readable by any script on the page, so any XSS vulnerability leaks the token — a bad trade for sensitive credentials. Whatever the storage, authorization must be enforced on the server; the client is never a security boundary.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The token-storage tradeoff between XSS exposure and convenience.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It's a frequent senior auth question and a real source of breaches.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: httpOnly cookies hide the token from script; localStorage exposes it.

theory.whyImportant: The wrong choice turns any XSS into full account takeover.

nestedTopics.title: SameSite + CSRF
nestedTopics.explanation: httpOnly cookies are auto-sent, so pair them with SameSite and/or CSRF tokens to stop forged requests.

followUps.question: If you use cookies, what new risk appears and how do you handle it?
followUps.answer: CSRF — mitigate with SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies, CSRF tokens on state-changing requests, and checking the Origin header.

keyTakeaways: Sessions keep state server-side (opaque cookie id); JWTs are stateless signed tokens.
Prefer httpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies over localStorage for sensitive tokens.
JWTs are hard to revoke — plan short expiry + refresh.
OAuth/OIDC delegates login so you never store passwords.
Always authorize on the server; the client UI is not a security boundary.
